Connecticut Senator Chris Murphy hospitalized after stroke
U.S. Senator Chris Murphy of Connecticut has been hospitalized after suffering a stroke, his office announced. The 53-year-old Democrat is awake and alert, and his staff is optimistic he will make a full recovery.
Murphy began experiencing numbness in his arm Saturday afternoon while attending his son’s hockey game, his chief of staff, Allison Herwitt, said in a statement Sunday. He was taken to a local hospital, where doctors determined he had suffered a stroke.
“He was transferred to Johns Hopkins for further monitoring and is responding well to treatment,” Herwitt said. “The doctors are encouraged by his progress, he is awake and alert, and we are optimistic he will make a full recovery.”
Murphy remains at Johns Hopkins Hospital in Baltimore. His office did not specify the type of stroke, the treatment he received or when he might be discharged.
A stroke occurs when blood flow to part of the brain is blocked or a blood vessel in the brain ruptures.
Sudden arm numbness or weakness is among the warning signs, along with difficulty speaking, vision changes and loss of balance, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). Rapid treatment can reduce brain damage.
Murphy has served in the Senate since January 2013 and was reelected to a third term in 2024. He previously served three terms in the U.S. House of Representatives.
He became a prominent advocate for tighter gun laws following the 2012 shooting at Sandy Hook Elementary School in Newtown, Connecticut, which was part of his congressional district.

Doctors there discovered he had experienced a stroke, and he was subsequently transferred to Johns Hopkins for further monitoring. Chief of staff Allison Herwitt said he was responding well to treatment, with his office optimistic that he would make a full recovery.

'The doctors are encouraged by his progress, he is awake and alert, and we are optimistic he will make a full recovery,' Herwitt said. No timetable was given for his discharge or return to Senate duties.

Pennsylvania Senator John Fetterman, who suffered a stroke during his 2022 election campaign, responded with a message drawing on his own experience.

Murphy, 53, experienced symptoms on Saturday while attending his son’s hockey game and was taken to a hospital. He was later transferred to another hospital and is expected to make a full recovery, according to his office.
“Yesterday afternoon, Sen. Murphy started experiencing numbness in his arm while at his son’s hockey game,” Murphy chief of staff Allison Herwitt said in a statement on Sunday.
“He was taken to a local hospital, where it was discovered he had experienced a stroke,” she said. “He was transferred to Johns Hopkins for further monitoring and is responding well to treatment. The doctors are encouraged by his progress, he is awake and alert, and we are optimistic he will make a full recovery.”
Murphy, who is not on Tuesday’s ballot, has been campaigning the past several weeks in Connecticut and a handful of swing states on behalf of Democratic candidates competing in the midterm elections. He was supposed to be in New Hampshire on Sunday to campaign with U.S. Rep. Chris Pappas, who’s running for Senate.
Speaking from a canvass launch in Meriden on Sunday afternoon, U.S. Rep. Jahana Hayes, D-5th District, gave a heartfelt shout-out to Murphy and the work he’s done for Democratic candidates across the country in recent weeks.
Hayes and a few other Connecticut Democrats on the ballot this Tuesday spoke to a group of a few dozen volunteers and supporters. Many of them gasped as Hayes broke the news.
“Today, I’m just struggling with the fact that everything is on the line. In two days, we will know the outcome in the House and in the Senate. I’m sure you’ve all heard this morning that Sen. Murphy suffered a stroke and he’s in the hospital,” Hayes said as the mood of the room quickly shifted to surprise and murmurs about the news.
“He has been all over this country working for Democratic candidates up and down the ballot because he understands it’s not just about what happens to those small things, it’s about making sure that those big things are also taken care of. It’s about making sure that we have Democratic majorities in the House and in the Senate. He’s going to be OK,” she said to applause.
Gov. Ned Lamont, at a campaign stop in West Hartford on Sunday, said just he’d spoken with someone in Murphy’s office and was “leaving him alone,” he said. “He’s better than yesterday and tomorrow will be better again.”

Comptroller Sean Scanlon is a former Murphy staffer.
